description: If you’re fascinated by space exploration and love uncovering interesting facts about NASA’s missions, or if you’re skilled in research, storytelling, Canva, Illustrator, Photoshop, Procreate, coding, or digital design, you’re welcome to join our team! Let’s explore the stories behind NASA’s equipment left on the Moon and Mars and bring these forgotten pieces of space history back to life.
summary:
We developed Echoes of Apollo, an interactive website that tells the stories of ten NASA machines abandoned on the Moon and Mars. They include the Apollo 11, 12 and 15 lunar modules, Surveyor 3, the Viking 1 lander, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity. Visitors can explore maps of both worlds, read each machine's mission, journey and legacy, and watch a live counter showing how long it has been silent.

The project answers the challenge "Abandoned but Not Forgotten" directly. We kept only discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars and left out active rovers and deep-space probes. Each machine gets its own story, drawn from NASA mission records and written in plain language, so that hardware left behind becomes something people can understand and remember.

This matters because exploration is usually remembered for its launches and landings, not for what stays behind. These machines still hold lessons about how we explored and what we learned. By telling their stories, we hope to keep that knowledge alive and inspire the next generation of explorers.
details:
Echoes of Apollo is a website that tells the stories of ten NASA machines left behind on the Moon and Mars. When a visitor opens it, a live counter shows how long each machine has been silent. From there they can explore interactive maps, read a full story for each machine, compare lifespans on a timeline, sort a table of mission records and take a short quiz. The site is built from NASA mission pages and NSSDCA records that we collected, and the counters recalculate each time the page loads, so the silence keeps growing.

The project gives people an easy way into mission history. It turns dry records into stories that anyone can follow, it works on computers and phones, and it is free to use with no sign-in. Every fact traces back to a NASA source. Our intended impact is to make people remember what happens after the launch and the landing. We want visitors, especially students, to see that exploration leaves lasting traces, and that those traces still teach us about the Moon and Mars.

We built the site with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the maps and timeline drawn in SVG. We used Google Fonts for the typography, NASA and JPL-Caltech images, and a looping background video from our project slide. The site is hosted on GitHub Pages with a custom domain, and it needs nothing more than an ordinary computer or phone. We also used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and refine the code and wording. If your event asks teams to disclose AI use, keep this sentence.

The project is creative because it focuses on silence instead of success. The "time since last contact" counter is the centerpiece, and each machine speaks in its own voice before the facts begin. The Moon map sits on a real photograph, and the timeline shows how long each machine worked and then how much longer it has been quiet.

Along the way we considered accuracy first, using only NASA sources and marking a few Mars positions and one date as approximate. We kept the scope to abandoned equipment, leaving out active rovers and deep-space probes. We tested the layout on small screens, made the buttons easy to tap, and made the site usable with a keyboard. We also wrote in plain language and credited every image to NASA.
